speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the fundamentals of the rule of law is that the Government and Parliament should be subject to being scrutinised and checked by an independent judiciary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One key aspect is that when Judges are appointed, they must have security of tenure, meaning that they cannot be removed from office until they reach a certain age or, in some countries, until they die.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such security assures Judges and the public they serve that cases are decided according to the law, fearlessly and without favour.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The call I am making is not new.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, why am I bringing this up again today?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, such an extension of security of the tenure was preferable to the current practice of reemploying Judges reaching 65 on short-term contracts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This observation which I share is purely from a system design perspective and not a comment on the actual behaviour of any Judge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The suggestion to move the age when tenure ends from 65 to 70 years is actually a very modest one, if one looks at how life expectancy in Singapore has changed over the decades.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Just consider that – in 1969, a Judge retiring at 65 years then, statistically had just a few more years to live.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, our life expectancy has drastically increased to 84 years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Australia and New Zealand, the retirement age of Judges is 70.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The same can be said for our Judges in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We last discussed this issue in the House three years ago, in the course of a debate on Bills that restructured the courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During that debate, several Members of Parliament, including myself, raised the topic of the tenure of Supreme Court Judges.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I argued then for the extension of the retirement age to 70, from a manpower utilisation perspective and in the context of Singaporeans having better health and living longer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In his round-up speech at that time, then-Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong basically said – and here I am paraphrasing – that our system should be judged by outcomes and "if it ain't broke, why fix it?" He highlighted that public trust in our judicial system was high, while in some other countries with higher retirement ages, judicial morale was low.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, with due respect, this does not address specifically why an extension of the age when tenure ends was neither feasible nor beneficial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In fact, Minister Tong himself stated, in the course of the debate, that the security of tenure for a Supreme Court Judge seeks to secure the independence of the Judge in judicial proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, would an extension from 65 to 70 years not be better from that perspective?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Judges aged 65 should continue to enjoy security of tenure and retire for good at 70.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What is important is that the system must work well as a whole and be relevant and suited to our own local context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The retirement age for Judges should not be slavishly copied from other countries and jurisdictions; they have their own considerations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In any case, when you do a survey, there is also no fixed or uniform practice across the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are jurisdictions other than Singapore, where Judges also have tenure until the age of 65.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are also jurisdictions where Judges have tenure until 70, or for life.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Each jurisdiction decides what works best for their own specific outcomes and their own local context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Singapore, coming onto the Supreme Court Bench is often a second career.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Most, if not all, of our Supreme Court Judges are lawyers who have distinguished themselves in private practice, public service or academia, before accepting an appointment onto the Bench.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is appropriate at that time, for a Judge to consider what his or her continued contributions should be and how that is best carried out.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some might feel that they are able to make a valuable contribution for a while more – and if so, they can discuss a further appointment with the Chief Justice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some might prefer to take a step back and only hear cases when rostered according to their own availability – and if so, an appointment as a Senior Judge may be suitable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Others may prefer to retire altogether and spend the next phase of their life on other endeavours.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim refers to this as a loss to the nation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think this system provides for there to be flexibility to deal with the specific individual and his or her specific preferences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I think it is in this way that, in fact, we retain their legal talent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as I have mentioned, most, if not all, of the practitioners, from practice or from academia, who are appointed as Supreme Court Judges have distinguished themselves in their previous practice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The current system, the one that we have, that is practiced, takes into account all of these specific circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as I have said, it gives us the flexibility and allows us to take into account the specific wishes of each of the Judges when they reach age 65.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, my question is, if this is ordinarily being offered to Judges upon reaching 65, why not simply extend the retirement age to 70, since "ordinarily", there will be an extension of the term of office?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification is that he mentioned that some Judges might want to leave the Court at 65, they may have other plans and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But is it not possible to design the system such that the tenure ends at 70, but Judges can have the election of retiring at 65 – I mean at their election?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the latter point, it is really a question of whether you decide to fix it at 65 or 70.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I have said, by that time, most, if not all, of the Judges, have spent at least – on average – about 15 years on the Bench.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the further extensions in the different forms that I have outlined, gives them the choice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that is not the same as mandating that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, ordinarily offered does not mean that in all these cases, it is accepted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is still an option for a Judge to take one or more of the routes that I have indicated, such as being appointed as a Senior Judge instead, or perhaps taking on a case, depending on his or her preference on the caseload schedule.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, do you wish to withdraw your amendment?
